chief_complaint: increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she caught a urinary tract infection or is experiencing bladder irritation from drinking too many energy drinks while studying.
concerns: She is worried that needing to urinate every hour will cause her to fail her upcoming university exams.
expectations: She hopes to get a rapid urine test and a short course of antibiotics so her bladder symptoms clear up quickly.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes confirming the diabetes type before starting metformin, dietary changes, and regular HbA1c monitoring, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Type 1 diabetes without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: young age of onset with significant weight loss or ketosis, signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, kussmaul breathing, fruity breath), or very high presenting glucose with dehydration or altered mental status.
management_principles: Confirm diabetes with plasma glucose and/or HbA1c, assess for ketosis and acute illness, and distinguish type 1 diabetes or other diabetes types before selecting treatment
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. HPI: insulin resistance, obesity.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
reference_soap.assessment: Symptomatic hyperglycemia is suspected; diabetes type and acute metabolic complications require assessment before labeling this as type 2 diabetes.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm diabetes with plasma glucose and HbA1c, obtain electrolytes/renal function, and assess blood or urine ketones and acid-base status when clinically indicated. Distinguish type 1 diabetes or other diabetes types before selecting treatment. Start lifestyle and pharmacologic therapy according to the confirmed diabetes type, glycemic severity, renal function, and pregnancy status; arrange prompt follow-up.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Implement evidence-based management plan: Metformin, dietary changes, regular HbA1c checks

teaching.one_liner: Insulin resistance, often related to obesity, causing increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue.
red_flags: Young age of onset with significant weight loss or ketosis — raises concern for type 1 diabetes or LADA rather than type 2
Signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath) — a medical emergency
Very high presenting glucose with dehydration or altered mental status — raises concern for hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

must_ask.say: How much are you drinking and urinating?
Does diabetes run in your family?
How long has this been going on?

history.answer: I've been feeling extremely thirsty all the time and having to pee constantly, and I just feel completely exhausted lately.
Every time I go to the bathroom, it's a very large amount of urine, not just small drops.
It started about three or four weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse.
I drink about four to five liters a day, mostly water, but also some iced tea or fruit juice because my throat feels so dry.
I wake up three or four times every night to use the bathroom.
Yes, I keep a large bottle of ice water right next to my bed because I wake up parched craving cold water.
My appetite has actually been slightly increased, and my weight has remained fairly steady with no noticeable drop.
No, I haven't had any nausea, vomiting, or stomach sickness.
No, I do not have any abdominal pain or stomach cramps.
No shortness of breath at all, and I don't feel confused or drowsy, just constantly tired.
I feel completely worn out and sluggish almost every day, even when I get eight hours of sleep.
Sometimes my vision gets slightly blurry towards the end of the day, but it comes and goes.
No, I haven't had skin boils, slow-healing scrapes, or vaginal yeast infections.
No, I have no burning, stinging, or pain when I pass urine.
No, I have never had a head injury, brain surgery, or persistent headaches.
No, I haven't had any constipation, bone aches, or kidney stones.
No, I don't have any muscle cramps, spasms, or muscle weakness.
No, I do not take lithium, water pills, steroids, or any diabetes drugs.
I drink one cup of coffee in the morning and never drink energy drinks.
No psychiatric conditions, and I'm not drinking water compulsively from stress; I'm genuinely parched.
My mother and my maternal grandfather both have type 2 diabetes.
I thought I might have picked up a urinary tract infection, or that I've been overdoing energy drinks while studying late.
I'm terrified that having to run to the restroom every hour will ruin my upcoming final exams.
I was hoping you could check my urine and give me some antibiotics so I can get back to studying.
I don't have any chronic illnesses or medical problems in my past.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps a glass of beer once or twice a month.
I am a university student living in an apartment near campus with a roommate.
My menstrual cycle is regular every 28 days, my last period was two weeks ago, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Patient is alert, well-nourished, and appears overweight, in no acute distress with normal respiratory effort and no fruity breath odor.
Blood pressure is 120/76 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Oral mucous membranes appear mildly dry; pharynx is clear without erythema or tonsillar enlargement.
Visual acuity is intact, extraocular movements are full, and confrontation visual fields are normal bilaterally.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, symmetric, and non-tender without palpable nodules or goiter.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular sounds and no wheezing or crackles.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no heart murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout with no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly.
Velvety, hyperpigmented thickening noted on the posterior neck consistent with acanthosis nigricans; normal skin turgor without open wounds or infections.
Light touch and pinprick sensation are completely intact and symmetric across both lower extremities and feet.
No pretibial or ankle edema bilaterally; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are full and symmetric.
